I. Introduction and Antimicrobial Therapy

Core definitions Lecture pp. 1–2

  • Drug: a chemical that produces a biological effect when administered to a living organism.
  • Antibiotic: from antibiosis, meaning “against life.” Historically, antibiotics were organic compounds produced by one microorganism that were toxic to other microorganisms. The lecture also describes the modern definition as including semi-synthetic compounds that selectively kill or inhibit microbial growth.
  • Antimicrobial: any substance of natural, semisynthetic, or synthetic origin that kills or inhibits the growth of microorganisms.
  • Antimicrobial is the broader term in the lecture. It can encompass antibacterial drugs, antimycobacterial drugs, antifungals, antivirals, antiprotozoals, and antihelminths.

Bactericidal

Directly kills bacteria.

Bacteriostatic

Primarily inhibits bacterial growth and replication, allowing the host immune system to clear the infection.

Five major antibacterial targets Lecture p. 1

Cell wallBacterial proteinsNucleic acidsMetabolic pathwaysCell membrane

Different antibiotic classes act at different points with the same overall goal: interfere with processes essential for bacterial survival or multiplication.

MIC, MBC, tolerance, and clinical risk Lecture p. 1

  • MIC: lowest antimicrobial concentration that prevents visible bacterial growth.
  • MBC: lowest concentration that kills the organism.
  • MBC:MIC ratio: the lecture uses it as a way to assess killing properties. The figure shows ≤ 4 with bactericidal activity and > 4 with bacteriostatic activity.
  • Tolerance: growth is suppressed, but bacterial killing is relatively ineffective. The figure associates tolerance with a very high MBC.
  • Predictable adverse effects: renal or hepatic toxicity.
  • Unpredictable adverse effects: immune-mediated hypersensitivity and idiosyncratic reactions.
  • Superinfection risk: broad-spectrum use can disrupt normal microbiota and predispose to Clostridioides difficile infection, fungal overgrowth, and candidiasis.
High-Yield RecapSuccessful therapy requires more than choosing a drug active against a microorganism.
Know how the drug acts and whether it inhibits or kills.
Know what concentration is required.
Know what toxicities may occur.
Know how resistance limits treatment.

Landmark moments Lecture p. 1

1928: Fleming. Penicillin from Penicillium notatum was observed to inhibit nearby bacteria.→ 1940: Florey and Chain. Penicillin was purified using freeze-drying technology. First human trials also took place in 1940.→ World War II. Mass production saved an estimated 12% to 15% of military lives from wound infections according to the lecture.→ 1943: Waksman. Streptomycin was discovered and described as the first antibiotic highly active against Gram-negative pathogens and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.→ 1945 Nobel Prize. Fleming, Florey, and Chain.

II. Antibiotic Classification

How the lecture classifies antibiotics Lecture pp. 2–3

  • Most common: spectrum of activity and mode of action.
  • Uncommon: route of administration and allergic potential, side effects, and toxicities.
A. According to effect on bacteria

Bactericidal antibiotics

  • Kill microorganisms and eradicate infection.
  • The lecture states there is no need for the body’s defense mechanisms.
  • Require actively proliferating microorganisms.
  • Have no or little effect in non-growing bacteria.
  • Kill at serum levels achievable in the patient.
  • Often preferred in the lecture for immunocompromised patients, organ-transplant recipients, children, and the elderly.

Bacteriostatic antibiotics

  • Stop growth and division.
  • Allow the body’s defense mechanism to eradicate the infection.
  • Arrest growth and replication at achievable serum levels.
  • Limit spread while host defenses attack, immobilize, and eliminate pathogens.
Exam TrapDo not combine bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics for the same bacterial species according to this lecture because they do not have additive or synergistic effects.

C–E. Other classification approaches
  • Mechanism of action: cell wall synthesis inhibition, protein synthesis inhibition, nucleic acid synthesis inhibition, metabolic pathway inhibition, and drugs affecting cell membrane permeability.
  • Route of administration: an uncommon classification. The lecture gives topical and oral as examples.
  • Allergic potential, side effects, and toxicities: another uncommon classification. The lecture notes that antibiotics in the same structural class may show similar patterns in these properties.

Mechanistic Targets and Bacterial Envelopes

Where antimicrobial drugs act Lecture p. 2

The lecture’s target map places antibacterial actions at the cell wall, ribosome, DNA and RNA machinery, folate pathway, and cytoplasmic membrane.

Figure 4, lecture p. 2. Site-of-action map showing major antimicrobial target locations and representative drug groups.

Gram-positive envelope Lecture p. 2

  • Thick, highly cross-linked peptidoglycan or murein mesh.
  • Provides shape and shields against mechanical and osmotic stress.
  • Higher peptidoglycan content and lower lipid concentration.
  • Retains crystal violet during solvent treatment.
  • Examples: Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus anthracis, and Clostridium botulinum.

Gram-negative envelope Lecture p. 3

  • An outer membrane provides an additional chemical barrier.
  • It prevents entry of many large or hydrophobic substances.
  • Porin channels permit entry of small hydrophilic molecules, including drugs, into the periplasmic space.
  • Periplasmic space lies between the outer and cytoplasmic membranes.
  • Examples: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Shigella, Yersinia pestis, and Salmonella species.
Figure 5, lecture p. 3. Structural comparison of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial envelopes.

III. Bacterial Cell Wall Synthesis

Peptidoglycan structure Lecture pp. 3 and 7

  • Peptidoglycan, also called murein in older sources, is the strong mesh-like layer surrounding the bacterial cell.
  • It is made of long sugar polymers.
  • The backbone contains alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) linked by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds.
  • Each NAM carries a short peptide chain or pentapeptide.
  • Bacteria continuously build and remodel this layer to remain alive.

PBPs and cross-linking

Transglycosylase
Adds NAG–NAM disaccharide-pentapeptide units and extends glycan strands→Transpeptidase
Cross-links peptide chains of adjacent strands→Removes terminal D-alanine→Remaining donor peptide cross-links to adjacent chain→Rigid peptidoglycan mesh

Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) coordinate extension of glycan strands and cross-linking while the cell grows and divides.

Must Knowβ-lactams bind PBPs and inhibit their activity.
No cross-linking → weak cell wall → cell lysis and bacterial death.
Figure 6, lecture pp. 3 and 7. Twelve-panel visual of peptidoglycan synthesis, transglycosylation, transpeptidation, cross-linking, and β-lactam interruption of PBPs.

β-lactamase enzymes Lecture p. 3

  • β-lactamases inactivate susceptible β-lactams by disrupting the β-lactam structure.
  • The lecture gives penicillinase as an example.
  • β-lactamase inhibitors protect the partner antibiotic from enzymatic destruction.
  • Examples: clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam.
Combinations named in the lecture
Amoxicillin + clavulanic acidAugmentin
Piperacillin + tazobactamZosyn
Cefoperazone + sulbactamSulperazone

Early versus late-stage cell wall inhibitors Lecture p. 3

Early stage

  • Act mainly during precursor production in the cytoplasm.
  • Fosfomycin inhibits MurA.
  • Cycloserine interferes with the D-Ala-D-Ala step.

Late stage

  • Interfere with assembly and cross-linking of mature peptidoglycan.
  • β-lactams inhibit PBPs and transpeptidation.
  • Vancomycin targets D-Ala-D-Ala.
  • Bacitracin inhibits lipid carrier recycling.
Figure 7, lecture p. 3. Early inhibitors stop precursor synthesis. Late inhibitors stop mature assembly and cross-linking.

IV-A. Ribosome as a Bacterial Target

Bacterial ribosome

70S total sedimentation coefficient.

  • 30S small subunit
  • 50S large subunit
  • 30 + 50 ≠ 70 because S values are sedimentation measurements, not simple additive quantities.

Human cytoplasmic ribosome

80S total.

  • 40S small subunit
  • 60S large subunit
  • The structural distinction helps antibiotics target bacteria selectively and minimize harm to human cells.

VI. Antimicrobial Resistance

Change the target→Block drug entry→Inactivate the drug→Pump the drug out
Four Primary Biochemical Pathways of Resistance
MechanismWhat the bacterium changesWhat happensLecture examples
Target ModificationActive drug site or binding targetMutations in active drug sites prevent binding.Ribosomal mutation reduces tetracycline or aminoglycoside affinity.
Altered PBPs render beta-lactams ineffective.
Mutated DNA gyrase resists quinolones.
Permeability ChangesMembrane porins or transport receptorsDrug entry is reduced or prevented.Porin loss in Gram-negative bacteria can block hydrophilic beta-lactams.
Diminished active uptake limits cytoplasmic aminoglycoside levels.
Inactivating EnzymesBacterial drug-modifying enzymesEnzymes physically degrade or chemically modify the antibiotic before it reaches its target.Beta-lactamases.
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (AGEs).
CAT or chloramphenicol acetyltransferase.
Transmembrane EffluxMembrane efflux proteinsDrug molecules are actively pumped out of the bacterial cytoplasm, preventing accumulation to toxic levels.Active efflux is highlighted for tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, and quinolones.
Study AidResistance = alter the target → limit entry → destroy or modify the drug → pump it out.
This is a memory arrangement of the lecture's four mechanisms.
Human Drivers of Global Resistance Lecture p. 5
What accelerates selective pressure?
DriverLecture point
Over-prescriptionSelective pressures are heavily accelerated by over-prescription of antibiotics.
Animal husbandry + hospital spreadMassive antibiotic use in animal husbandry and spread of multidrug-resistant strains in hospitals due to unhygienic practices multiply global pathogen resistance.
Unnecessary antibiotic exposureThe lecturer describes unnecessary exposure as allowing organisms to repeatedly encounter the drugs and develop ways to resist them.
Prolonged courses + inadequate dosingUnnecessarily prolonged courses and inadequate dosing can promote bacterial resistance.
Broad spectrum when not neededPrescribing a broad-spectrum antibiotic when it is not needed can promote resistance.
Judicious broad-spectrum useBroader initial coverage may be used for difficult-to-treat disease or septic shock, but the lecture says to reassess after 2–3 days using culture and susceptibility testing.
Broad empiric coverage
when justified→Culture + susceptibility→Reassess at 2–3 days→De-escalate
when appropriate
Clinical Interventions & Stewardship
Resistance-Control Measures in the Lecture
StrategyLecture action
Restrict antibiotic usePreserve specialized broad-spectrum agents such as carbapenems or linezolid for severe, documented infections.
Infection preventionInfection prevention is equally important aside from prescribing.
Constant exposure controlsExpose bacterial colonies to sustained, high concentrations to completely eradicate pathogens and prevent mutant survival.
Antibiotic stewardshipPrevent both re-emergence of organisms and their transmission.
Multiple-agent regimensCombination therapies with different mechanisms of action are presented as a way to halt resistance.
Strategic preservationHygienic lifestyle and sterile hospital environments restrict survival and transmission of dangerous hospital-selected strains.
Must KnowDo not leave broad empiric therapy on autopilot.
When culture and susceptibility results become available, reassess the regimen and move toward the narrowest effective agent when appropriate.

Cram Sheet

Definitions

  • Antimicrobial: natural, semisynthetic, or synthetic substance that kills or inhibits microorganisms.
  • Antibiotic: historically microorganism-derived. Modern lecture framing includes semisynthetic compounds.
  • MIC: prevents visible growth.
  • MBC: kills organism.
  • Tolerance: growth suppressed but killing ineffective.

MBC:MIC cue

≤ 4 → bactericidal activity
> 4 → bacteriostatic activity
Very high MBC → tolerance

Cidal vs Static

Cidal kills.
Static stops growth.

Exam TrapDo not combine them for the same bacterial species according to this lecture.

Spectrum

Narrow: isoniazid.
Extended: ampicillin.
Broad: tetracycline.
Broader is not automatically better.

Cell wall core

NAG ↔ NAM by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds.
Transglycosylase extends glycan strands.
Transpeptidase cross-links peptide chains.
β-lactams bind PBPs → no cross-linking → weak wall → lysis.

Early vs Late wall inhibitors

Early: fosfomycin → MurA. Cycloserine → D-Ala-D-Ala step.
Late: β-lactams → PBPs. Vancomycin → D-Ala-D-Ala. Bacitracin → lipid carrier recycling.

β-lactamase rescue

Clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam protect the partner drug.
Amoxicillin + clavulanate.
Piperacillin + tazobactam.
Cefoperazone + sulbactam.

Ribosome map

Bacteria 70S = 30S + 50S.
Humans 80S = 40S + 60S.
S values are not simply additive.

30S

Aminoglycosides: irreversible, oxygen-dependent entry, mRNA misreading, bactericidal.
Tetracyclines: reversible, block aminoacyl-tRNA at A-site, bacteriostatic.

50S

Macrolides and lincosamides: translocation or elongation arrest.
Chloramphenicol: peptidyl transferase blockade.
Oxazolidinones: prevent 70S initiation complex.

Nucleic acid

Fluoroquinolones: DNA gyrase or topoisomerase II and topoisomerase IV → bactericidal.
Rifamycins: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase → bactericidal.

Folate

Sulfonamides → dihydropteroate synthase.
Trimethoprim → dihydrofolate reductase.
Co-trimoxazole blocks both steps.

PK anchors

Tetracyclines: 75%–100% oral BA. Food or divalent cations may reduce absorption 50%.
Aminoglycosides: virtually unabsorbed orally for systemic use. Monitor serum creatinine.
Macrolides: extensive tissue penetration.
β-lactams: mainly renal, except ceftriaxone and cefoperazone biliary.

Resistance: 4 ways

Modify target.
Reduce permeability.
Inactivate drug.
Efflux drug.

Stewardship

Use broad-spectrum agents judiciously.
Reassess after 2–3 days with culture and susceptibility when applicable in the lecture framework.
De-escalate to the narrowest effective agent.

Lecture summary

Chemotherapy is described as selective use of drugs to eradicate pathogenic microorganisms.
Antibiotic classification centers on target organism, spectrum, cidal versus static effect, and mechanism of action.

Source basis: Introduction to Antimicrobials V1, Pharmacology Trans 2.07. Content is organized from the lecture only.
